title: Hildegard of Bingen
hookLine: abbess, composer, healer: she saw God's greening power in all living things

lines: A NUN GIVES IT A NAME.
cards: The first warm week of spring arrives, and the whole world seems to have turned on overnight.
The trees are hazy with new leaves, the grass is a green so bright it almost hurts, and even the weeds in the sidewalk cracks look proud of themselves. Something is pushing up out of everything.
In a German convent long ago, a nun gave that pushing a name. She was a composer, a healer, a writer of visions, a letter-writer to emperors and popes.
And she believed the green in the grass was saying something about God. Today's word: viriditas.

teach.h: A CHILD GIVEN TO A MONASTERY.
teach.b: Hildegard of Bingen was born in the Rhineland. As a child she was given to a monastery, and she lived her whole life in a Benedictine community, under yesterday's Rule.
By her own account she had seen visions of light since she was small, but told almost no one.

Then, in her early forties, she says she heard a command to write down what she saw. She hesitated, doubting herself, and fell ill, and only recovered once she began to write. The book became Scivias, Know the Ways.
After that, she seemed to do everything. She founded her own convent. She wrote music that is still sung and recorded today, soaring chants, and a sung drama about the virtues.
She wrote about plants and medicine and the human body. She wrote to bishops, abbots, emperors and popes, and wasn't shy about telling them what she thought.
Running through all of it is one Latin word: viriditas, from viridis, green. Greenness.
For Hildegard, it meant the life force of God flowing through creation, the sap in the tree, the health in a body, the freshness in a soul. A person dry and tired inside had lost their greenness.
When grace moved in them, they grew green again. Christians find the picture in the Bible too: the righteous like a tree planted by the rivers of water, whose leaf does not wither.
For Hildegard, the green outside and the life of God inside were not two different things.
In 2012, Pope Benedict XVI named her a Doctor of the Church, a title the Catholic Church gives to teachers whose writing it holds up for the whole church.

how: Christians and others sing Hildegard's music and read her visions, and some find in her idea of viriditas a way to see God's life in the natural world; Catholics keep her feast day on September 17.

games.q: you're a nun in your early forties. you've seen visions of light since childhood and told almost no one. now you hear: write what you see. what do you do?
o: write it all down that night.
games.why: by her own account she hesitated, fell ill, and recovered only once she began to write. the book was Scivias.

practice: Touch something green: a houseplant, a leaf outside the door, the herbs in the kitchen, a blade of grass; if nothing green is near, picture one clearly.
Feel it, cool and alive, still pushing, still growing, and then gently ask: where in me feels dry right now? If you pray, you can offer that dry place.

wordCard.voice: Viriditas. Latin: greenness. Hildegard's word for God's life pushing up through everything that lives.

orig.note: Latin: greenness, from viridis, green; Hildegard's word for God's life in creation.

carryVoice: Your line: the greening. For Hildegard, what's dry can grow green again. Day two hundred sixty-seven.
